title: Evaluating the cost asymmetry of Type I vs Type II errors in business
scenario_markdown:
A food processing enterprise tests daily production batches of baby formula for bacterial pathogen contamination before release to grocery distribution networks. The quality assurance team establishes the following testing hypotheses:

$$H_0: \text{Batch is safe (free of harmful pathogens)}$$
$$H_1: \text{Batch is contaminated (pathogen present)}$$

Meanwhile, the marketing department runs an A/B test on promotional email subject lines where $H_0: \text{No difference in open rate}$ vs $H_1: \text{Subject line B increases open rate}$.

parameters.objective: Evaluate asymmetric business costs of Type I and Type II errors to drive testing design

assumptions: Test decisions carry distinct business, legal, and operational consequences
Hypotheses reflect standard status quo vs discovery framing

approval.notes: Reviewed conceptual question on the practical cost asymmetry between Type I and Type II errors. Demonstrates why statistical design (alpha and sample size/power) is driven by the real-world penalty of making the more dangerous error.

stages.prompt_markdown: In the baby formula pathogen test, identify what a Type II error represents and evaluate its business and ethical consequence compared to a Type I error.

options.text_markdown: Type II error: Failing to reject $H_0$ when the batch is actually contaminated (shipping contaminated formula to consumers). This is far worse than Type I (scrapping a safe batch), as it risks severe infant illness, loss of life, and catastrophic corporate liability.
Type II error: Rejecting $H_0$ when the batch is safe (destroying safe formula), which is worse because of immediate financial inventory loss.
options.hint_markdown: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is a Type I error (false positive), not a Type II error.

options.text_markdown: Both errors carry identical consequences because probability theory treats $\alpha$ and $\beta$ symmetrically.
options.hint_markdown: While $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are both probabilities, their real-world costs and liabilities are heavily asymmetric in almost all business and medical applications.

options.text_markdown: Type I error is always worse in every business application by definition of the scientific method.
options.hint_markdown: In safety, toxicity, and fraud detection, failing to catch a hazard (Type II error) is typically far more dangerous than a false alarm (Type I error).

stages.explanation_markdown: A Type I error is rejecting $H_0$ when $H_0$ is true (false alarm: flagging a safe batch as contaminated and scrapping it). A Type II error is failing to reject $H_0$ when $H_0$ is false (missed hazard: failing to detect pathogens and shipping contaminated formula). Because shipping dangerous formula causes severe public health harm and massive lawsuits, Type II error is dramatically more perilous in this setting.

stages.prompt_markdown: How should the engineering leadership design the testing protocol when a Type II error is catastrophic?

options.text_markdown: Design the test with high statistical power ($1 - \beta \ge 0.99$), use larger sample volumes, and allow a higher significance level $\alpha$ (e.g., $0.05$ or $0.10$) if necessary to minimize $\beta$.
Set $\alpha$ as close to zero as possible (e.g., $\alpha = 0.0001$) while keeping the sample size small.
options.hint_markdown: Shrinking $\alpha$ with fixed sample size makes the rejection threshold harder to cross, which directly increases $\beta$ (the probability of a Type II error!).

options.text_markdown: Focus exclusively on the $p$-value and ignore sample size and power altogether.
options.hint_markdown: Without adequate sample size and power, a small-sample test cannot reliably detect low-concentration pathogens.

options.text_markdown: Apply the exact same test standards used in the marketing email A/B test because $\alpha = 0.05$ is a universal legal mandate.
options.hint_markdown: The value $\alpha = 0.05$ is a convention, not a mandate; risk-sensitive domains adjust $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $n$ to reflect domain costs.

stages.explanation_markdown: When Type II error carries immense risk, the priority is minimizing $\beta$ (maximizing power $1 - \beta$). Quality teams achieve this by investing in larger sample sizes $n$ and accepting a higher false alarm rate $\alpha$ if necessary, ensuring that dangerous contamination is virtually never missed.
